c1.story:
Pick up the towel in your bathroom. If you bought it at a big-box store in America, there is a decent chance it was woven in Gujarat or Punjab. The bedsheet in a London department store, the knitted T-shirt on a Paris high street, the innerwear in your own cupboard: Indian textile companies are all over them, mostly without their names on the label.

India has a textile tradition older than almost any other industry on this page, and it is one of the country's biggest employers. But as an investment, textiles is not one business. It is four, sitting at different points between a cotton field and a shop shelf, and they keep very different slices of the money.

Door one is fibre and yarn. Vardhman in Punjab, Filatex and Sanathan making polyester, Alok: they sell yarn or synthetic fibre by the kilo to other mills, at a market price. Their profit is the gap between what cotton or polyester costs and what yarn fetches, and they control neither side.

Door two is the export maker. Welspun Living, Indo Count, Gokaldas Exports and Pearl Global make towels, bedsheets and garments to order for Western retailers' own labels. The retailer's name goes on the product; the Indian company's name goes on the invoice.

Door three is the integrated mill. KPR Mill, Arvind, Trident and Jindal Worldwide own several stages of the chain, from yarn to fabric to finished garment or towel, so the margin at one stage feeds the next.

Door four is where the pricing power lives. Page Industries sells Jockey innerwear in India under licence, and the shopper pays for the name. Garware Technical Fibres makes engineered nets and fabrics for fish farms and sports grounds, sold on performance.

In textiles, the closer you get to your own brand, the more of each rupee you keep.
c1.read:
Four tiles, one per door. Read each from top to bottom, then compare the profit bars from left to right. They tell a single story.

  • The line under the name says how the product is sold. Yarn by the kilo at a market price. Goods made to order for a Western retailer's label. A chain owned end to end. Or a brand and an engineered product sold on name and performance.
  • The tickers open each company's page. Some names straddle doors: TRIDENT, on the integrated tile, is also a big towel exporter, and WELSPUNLIV has its own brands alongside its retailer business. Value the pieces separately.
  • The profit bar climbs as you move right: low for fibre and yarn, medium for exporters and integrated mills, high for brands and technical textiles. This is exactly the line the so-what states: the further a company sits from raw fibre and the closer to its own brand, the more it keeps.
  • The bet line spells out what you are buying: a cotton-to-yarn spread, Western shoppers plus trade deals plus the rupee, full mills run cheaply, or pricing power.

Notice that two very different tiles both read medium. The exporters earn their middle slice from relationships with big retailers, which can be lost. The integrated mills earn theirs from efficiency across the chain, which is harder to lose but needs full factories. Same bar, different risks.

Before reading anything else, put each textile name you own on a tile. The cotton price means opposite things for the first two.

c2.story:
The textile kitchen starts in a field. At station one, cotton is grown across Gujarat, Maharashtra, Telangana and Punjab, picked and ginned to separate fibre from seed. Alongside it, polyester is made from oil-derived chemicals and viscose from wood pulp. The Cotton Corporation of India buys from farmers whenever prices fall below the government's support price, which is why Indian cotton can sometimes cost more than cotton elsewhere in the world.

Station two is spinning, where fibre is twisted into yarn on spindles that run day and night. This is India's strongest station. Vardhman, KPR Mill, Trident and hundreds of smaller mills across Tamil Nadu, Gujarat and Punjab make so much yarn that India exports it, much of it historically to China and Bangladesh.

Station three is fabric: weaving or knitting yarn into cloth, then dyeing and finishing it. Arvind is famous for denim; Jindal Worldwide and Alok are big here too. But this is where China looms largest. Chinese mills make a huge share of the world's fabric, with scale, integration and dyeing capacity that Indian mills struggle to match.

Station four is making up: cutting and stitching fabric into garments, towels and bedsheets. Here India splits in two. In home textiles, India is a world leader: Welspun, Indo Count and Trident supply towels and bedsheets to the biggest American retailers. In garments, Bangladesh and Vietnam have beaten India for years, thanks to lower wages, giant factories and duty-free access to Europe that India lacked.

Station five is the brand and the shelf, mostly Western retailers for exports, Page Industries and Indian brands at home.

So the Indian kitchen is strong at the start, contested in the middle and weak at the end: great at yarn and towels, outgunned in fabric and garments.
c2.read:
Read the diagram in two passes: the station boxes left to right, then the two band rows.

The five boxes run from fibre to shelf. Each says what happens and who does it. Notice the cast change: farmers, the Cotton Corporation and synthetic fibre makers at station one; Indian spinners at two; Arvind and Jindal Worldwide at three, with a note that China dominates world fabric; Welspun, Indo Count and Gokaldas at four, with Bangladesh and Vietnam competing hard; Western retailers and Page at five.

The first band row labels who holds each station, and it is unusually candid. Stations one and two are Indian: fibre makers and Indian spinners. Station three is labelled China's fabric, marked as a rival. Station four is Bangladesh and Vietnam, also rivals. Station five is global retailers. In other words, the band row admits that Indian listed companies do not hold the middle and later stations, even though some of them operate there.

The second band row shows the rival across the producing stations, as labelled: China, with Bangladesh and Vietnam in garments, and World under the shelf.

The note underneath gives the geography: spinning near the cotton belt in Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Punjab; garments and home textiles in Tiruppur, Panipat, Karur and Bengaluru. The so-what line draws the conclusion: because Indian listed names are strongest upstream and in home textiles, their fortunes swing with cotton prices and Western orders.

Use it to trace news. A bad monsoon hits station one first. A US tariff hits stations four and five. A trade deal that gives Indian garments the same access as Bangladesh's changes who wins at station four.

c3.story:
If you want to know how Welspun Living's next quarter will go, do not start with Welspun. Start with an American retailer's warehouse.

That is because the listed exporters depend heavily on a handful of large US retailers, the big-box chains and department stores that sell towels and bedsheets under their own labels. When those retailers' shelves are lean, they place big orders. When their warehouses are full of unsold stock, as they were in 2022 and 2023, orders dry up for months, regardless of how many towels American shoppers are actually buying. It is the same destocking pattern you see in chemicals: the middleman's inventory, not the end customer's appetite, drives the order book.

That concentration can be brutal. In 2016, a major American retailer dropped Welspun after discovering that sheets sold as Egyptian cotton were not, and the stock fell sharply. One customer's decision moved an entire listed company.

Beyond the US, there are European and UK apparel brands buying T-shirts, denim and knitwear to order, increasingly as part of a China plus one strategy: buyers adding a second supplier outside China. The US ban on cotton from China's Xinjiang region, which came into force in 2022, gave that strategy extra urgency. The UK is about to matter more, thanks to the new trade pact.

At home, Indian shoppers buy innerwear, ethnic wear and everyday clothes, moving with rural and urban spending and, crucially, the wedding season. Other mills, in India and abroad, buy yarn. Industrial buyers want fishing nets and agricultural textiles. The government buys uniforms.

For an Indian towel exporter, an American warehouse manager is the most important economist in the world.
c3.read:
Each tile is one customer group: who buys, what they buy, and what moves them. Sort the tiles by where they sit and you will see the industry's exposure clearly.

  • The export tiles: US home-furnishing retailers, US and European apparel brands, and UK retailers. Their third lines are the global drivers: US housing activity, tariffs on Indian goods, store inventories, China plus one sourcing and the India-UK pact. Three of seven tiles, but most of the listed exporters' revenue.
  • The domestic tile: Indian shoppers, moving with spending and the wedding season. This is where Page Industries and the Indian brands live.
  • The intermediate tile: other mills, buying yarn, moving with Chinese and Bangladeshi demand. This is the spinners' customer, which is why China's yarn imports appear on the lead-time chart on card eleven.
  • The specialist tiles: industrial buyers of fishing nets, sports fabric and agricultural textiles, moving with aquaculture, infrastructure and farm spending; and government uniform tenders. These are Garware's world and a sliver of others'.

The most important tile is the first. Its third line names US tariffs on Indian goods, and the so-what line underneath warns that a US tariff or US inventory glut hits the exporters fast.

To use the grid, map each company. A towel and bedsheet exporter sits almost entirely on the first tile. A spinner sits on the yarn tile. A brand sits on the domestic tile. The more concentrated the map, the more one customer's cycle becomes your stock's cycle.

c4.story:
A spinning mill is a lot like a sugar mill. It buys its crop once a year, in season, stores it for months, processes it through the year and hopes the selling price holds. Get the cotton purchase right and the year is good. Buy at the top, as many mills did in 2022 when cotton spiked, and the inventory losses can wipe out a year's profit when prices fall.

That is why raw material is the line that matters most for a spinner: cotton or polyester is by far the biggest cost, and the spread between that cost and the yarn price is the whole business. Power comes next. Spindles run around the clock, and state power tariffs decide who can compete; a mill in a state with cheap industrial power has a real edge over one paying more. Working capital ties up cash because cotton bought in season sits in godowns for months, and interest on those working capital loans is what makes weak mills fragile when margins fall.

A brand's profit and loss looks completely different. Raw material is a much smaller share of sales, because the shopper is paying for the name, the fit and the trust, not the cotton. But the brand spends heavily on what the spinner barely needs: marketing, distribution, retail staff, a network of shops and dealers. Page Industries' innerwear sells for far more than the fabric in it costs, and that difference is the brand.

Then a line that only exporters fully appreciate: export incentives. Schemes that refund taxes embedded in exported textiles and garments can be worth a few percentage points of sales. For a thin-margin exporter, that can be the difference between profit and loss, which is why every change to those schemes makes headlines in Tiruppur.

A spinner bets on the cotton crop. A brand bets on the shopper. Their accounts look like two different industries.
c4.read:
Two charts walk one hundred rupees of sales down to what is left: fibre and yarn makers on one side, brands and technical textiles on the other. Read each left to right, and the contrast is the lesson.

  • The input bar is cotton and fibre. For the yarn maker it swallows roughly two-thirds of every rupee. For the brand it takes about four rupees in ten.
  • The opex bar is power, wages and freight. This flips: the brand's opex is double the spinner's, at over a third of sales, because selling a brand means people, shops, marketing and distribution.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is small for both, a bit bigger for the yarn maker, whose spindles are capital-intensive and who borrows to carry cotton.
  • The last bar is what is left. The yarn maker keeps less than a tenth. The brand keeps more than twice as much. Spending more on people and marketing, the brand still ends up with a far bigger slice: that is pricing power, seen on a chart.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts. Hover a bar for the rupee amount.

Below the charts, the line list marks what to watch. Raw material, power, working capital, capex and interest all get a yes: four of those five are about the spinner's cotton-and-spindle economics. Employee cost, depreciation and export incentives are sometimes. Employee cost is minor for a spinner but large for a garment maker who stitches by hand. Export incentives are minor for a domestic brand and potentially decisive for an exporter.

c5.story:
The textile cycle of the last six years has had more plot twists than most: a pandemic, a boom, a bust, a political upheaval in a rival country, a tariff shock and a trade-deal rescue.

In 2020 the lockdown shut mills and export orders vanished for months. Then 2021 and 2022 brought a boom. Western retailers restocked aggressively after the pandemic, and buyers shifted orders away from China, worried about supply disruptions and, from 2022, the US ban on Xinjiang cotton. Yarn prices hit records, and spinners made more money than they had in years.

The peak in 2022 came with a trap. Cotton spiked, and mills bought at the top, expecting the boom to continue. It did not. Western retailers discovered their warehouses were overflowing with unsold stock and slashed orders. Cotton crashed, and mills holding expensive inventory booked heavy losses. Through 2023 and 2024 the industry sat at the bottom: thin margins, slow orders and idle spindles at the smaller mills.

In 2024 came an unexpected boost: political upheaval in Bangladesh, which ended with Sheikh Hasina's ouster in August, pushed some garment orders to Indian makers. Then 2025 delivered a fresh blow. The US imposed steep tariffs on Indian goods, among the highest it charged any trading partner, and Indian exporters cut prices and lost orders to Bangladesh, Vietnam and others. The government waived its import duty on cotton for the second half of the year to give mills some relief.

By 2026 things had turned. The US cut its tariff under an interim deal, the UK pact brought duty-free access and the EU deal was concluded. Spinning margins recovered as synthetic fibre got dearer, making cotton yarn more competitive. The catch: US orders were still rebuilding.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock shows four arcs, clockwise from the top: boom, peak, bust and bottom. The years under each are from the last cycle: boom in 2021 and 2022, peak in 2022, bust from 2022 into 2023, bottom across 2023 and 2024. The arrow points to today, just short of twelve o'clock, at the end of the bottom arc and about to enter boom: an early up-cycle. Hover an arc for what defined it.

The timeline is where this industry's story gets interesting. Read the colours: the pandemic bust of 2020, the boom, the bust of 2022 and 2023, a neutral 2024 when Bangladesh's turmoil sent orders to India, then a second bust colour in 2025 for the US tariffs, and finally the now entry for 2026. That 2025 entry is a double dip that the four-arc clock cannot show on its own: the industry left the bottom, got knocked back by policy, and is now climbing again.

The four hands let you read the clock yourself.

  • Cotton price: high and firm, arrow up. Good for spinners' selling prices, a squeeze on garment and home-textile makers.
  • US orders to India: recovering slowly, a diamond. This is the trigger for exporters' earnings, and it has not fired yet.
  • Yarn spread: wider than last year, arrow up. Spinning margins are back.
  • Rupee: firmer this month, arrow down for the industry, because a stronger rupee cuts exporters' earnings per dollar.

Two up, one mixed, one down: an early up-cycle that is real for spinners and still pending for exporters.

c6.story:
A textile exporter in Tiruppur or Karur is plugged into a wiring diagram that runs through Washington, the cotton fields of Gujarat, the oil market and the currency desk.

Three dials carry three dots each. The first is the rupee against the dollar. Exporters earn in dollars and pay most costs in rupees, so a weaker rupee directly fattens their margins, and on thin margins a few percent of currency move is a big swing in profit. The second is US tariffs on Indian goods. Textiles is a price-sensitive business, and US retailers will move orders to Bangladesh or Vietnam over a small price gap. When the US raised tariffs on Indian goods sharply in 2025, that gap became a chasm, and orders moved. When it cut them in 2026, the door reopened. The third is the cotton price, a classic two-faced dial: rising cotton lifts spinners' selling prices briefly but squeezes the garment and home-textile makers who buy their yarn and fabric.

The two-dot dials include crude oil, which drives polyester and nylon costs. When crude rises, synthetic fibre gets dearer and cotton yarn becomes relatively more attractive, which is part of why spinning margins recovered recently. India's overall export momentum signals fuller mills. And interest rates matter more here than in many industries, because mills borrow heavily to carry cotton stock for months.

The one-dot dials are domestic: clothing inflation, which tells you whether brands can raise prices at home, and factory output, a general read on domestic demand.

Notice what dominates: two of the three heaviest dials are about the export trade, the currency and the tariff. That tells you where the industry's fate is really decided: not in Indian shops, but at Western ports.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across: the dial, the channel, what a rise does and the weight.

  • The arrows: green for the rupee row, India's exports, clothing inflation and factory output. Red for US tariffs and interest rates. A diamond for cotton and crude, which help one part of the industry and hurt another.
  • A note on the rupee row: its green arrow refers to a rise in the dollar-rupee rate, which means a weaker rupee. A weaker rupee helps exporters. If you see the rupee strengthening in the news, read it as the dial falling, which hurts.
  • Weight: three dots on the rupee, US tariffs and cotton. Two on crude, exports and interest rates. One on clothing inflation and factory output.

The latest column shows live readings where a dial maps to a series we track: the dollar-rupee rate, Brent crude, India's exports, clothing and footwear inflation, the policy rate and manufacturing output. US tariffs and cotton show a dash: tariffs move by announcement, and cotton is best followed through the Cotton Corporation and global cotton quotes.

The quickest use of the table: scan the three-dot rows first. Then, as the so-what line suggests, pair the rupee with US tariffs. Together they decide whether an Indian exporter is price-competitive in America. A lower tariff with a weaker rupee is the best combination; a higher tariff with a stronger rupee is the worst. Today, the tariff has come down but the rupee hand on card five is firmer, so the two are partly offsetting.

c7.story:
India grows cotton, spins excellent yarn, has a deep pool of skilled workers and a centuries-old textile tradition. So why did Bangladesh, with no cotton of its own, overtake India in garment exports? The bottlenecks explain it.

The first is fragmentation. India's textile industry is made up of thousands of small mills and units, many family-run. In a downturn, they all cut prices to keep their machines running, so nobody holds margin. Bangladesh, by contrast, built giant garment factories that could take the enormous orders Western retailers like to place.

The second is input cost. Quality control orders on imported polyester and viscose, meant to protect Indian fibre makers, keep synthetic fibre prices in India above Chinese levels. That helps the fibre maker and hurts every garment maker downstream who has to buy that fibre.

Then the farm. Indian cotton yields per acre are well below those of other big growers, so the crop is vulnerable to bad monsoons and pests like the pink bollworm, and a short crop sends prices soaring. Most garment makers are too small to win the giant orders Bangladesh and Vietnam take; this is improving slowly as integrated parks and incentives push scale.

Customer concentration cuts both ways. A few large US retailers buy most of India's home textiles, which gives the exporters big, steady volumes, but it means one buyer's mood can move a whole stock.

In textiles, the downturn does not kill the weak mills. It is the cotton they bought before the downturn that does.

And finally, cash stuck in cotton. Mills must buy in season and hold it for months. When prices fall, the inventory losses and working capital loans can sink a weak balance sheet.
c7.read:
Each row is one bottleneck, with why it bites and a severity label. The label tells you how to think about each risk.

  • Structural: fragmented small mills and pricier fibre than China. These are permanent features that cap the whole industry's returns. Fragmentation means no pricing discipline in downturns. Pricier fibre means Indian garments start every race a step behind Chinese ones.
  • Recurring: low cotton yields. A bad monsoon or a pest attack spikes cotton prices every few years. Expect it; do not be surprised by it.
  • Slow: small garment units. This is slowly improving as integrated parks and incentive schemes push companies to scale up, but it takes years.
  • Two-sided: US customer concentration. Big, loyal customers are a strength in good times and a single point of failure in bad times.
  • Cyclical: cash stuck in cotton. Harmless when cotton is rising, dangerous when it falls, as the 2022 crash showed.

The so-what underneath draws the conclusion: scale and cheap inputs decide survival, and the integrated mills with strong balance sheets come out of each bust stronger.

A useful way to use the table: for each company you own, check which rows it has escaped. An integrated mill with a strong balance sheet has largely escaped the fragmentation and cash rows. A brand has escaped most of them. A small spinner is exposed to almost every one.

c8.story:
Textiles has one of the busiest rulebooks of any Indian industry, and right now it is the trade rules, not the domestic ones, that are driving the story.

Start at home with cotton. The Cotton Corporation of India buys from farmers whenever prices fall below the minimum support price. That protects farmers, but it can put a floor under domestic cotton that keeps it above world prices, which hurts the mills. The customs duty on imported cotton adds to that. When the government waives it, as it did from August to the end of 2025 to cushion the US tariff blow, mills can import cheaper cotton and margins improve.

Then the incentives. Export duty rebate schemes refund taxes embedded in exported textiles and garments. A production-linked incentive scheme pays for new man-made fibre and technical textile capacity. And PM MITRA parks offer large integrated textile parks with shared infrastructure, an attempt to give Indian companies the scale that Bangladesh and Vietnam enjoy.

But the rows that matter most today are trade deals. The US reciprocal tariff decides whether American retailers buy from India or from its rivals, and its swings in 2025 and 2026 were the biggest single influence on exporters' stocks. The India-UK trade pact gives Indian textiles duty-free entry into Britain, putting Indian makers on level terms with Bangladesh there for the first time. And the India-EU agreement, concluded and awaiting ratification, will do the same for Europe.

For a decade, Indian garment makers ran the race with weights on. The trade deals are taking some of the weights off.

Bangladesh's advantage in Europe was never just cheaper labour. It was duty-free access that India lacked. That gap is now closing.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule. Read across: who it is, what it does, why you care and its status. This rulebook has more live rows than most; the status column helps you sort them.

  • Always: the Cotton Corporation and the support price, and the export duty rebates. Permanent background. The rebate row matters disproportionately to thin-margin exporters.
  • Live: the cotton import duty, the fibre quality control orders, the PLI scheme, PM MITRA parks and the US reciprocal tariff. Five live rows. The tariff row is the most important on the page; the cotton duty and fibre quality rows decide input costs.
  • New: the India-UK trade pact. Duty-free access to Britain is a real, immediate advantage for companies with UK customers, which is why the call prefers exporters with UK and European reach.
  • Coming: the India-EU agreement. Once ratified, it removes EU duties on Indian textiles. The biggest future swing factor.

Notice how many rows pull in opposite directions. The support price and fibre quality orders raise input costs; the duty waiver and incentive schemes lower them. The trade deals open markets; the US tariff can close one.

A practical habit: for each company, tick the rows that touch it. A US home-textile exporter is most exposed to the tariff row. A UK-focused garment maker benefits most from the new pact. A domestic brand barely touches the trade rows at all.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Porter's five forces asks who keeps the profit: rivals, suppliers, buyers, new entrants or substitutes. Few industries show the answer as starkly as textiles.

A yarn maker faces near-maximum pressure from almost every direction. Rivalry is relentless, because yarn is a commodity sold by thousands of mills, and in a downturn they all cut prices together. Buyers have all the power: a weaving mill shops on price and switches suppliers for a small saving. Suppliers are a mixed bag, since cotton follows the crop and the support price, which the spinner cannot influence. New entrants are a constant threat, because a small mill is cheap to start. Only substitutes offer relief: clothes themselves have no substitute, and cotton and polyester simply substitute for each other.

A brand faces almost the opposite. Page Industries does not compete with thousands of mills; it competes with a few other innerwear brands, on name and fit. It buys finished fabric and can switch mills, so suppliers have little power. Its buyer, the shopper, pays for the name and rarely haggles. New entrants face a long climb, because building a trusted brand, or a technical product that a fish farm or a stadium will rely on, takes years.

That gap in bargaining power is the single most important structural fact about this industry. It explains why a spinner and a brand, which both turn cotton into something, earn such different margins and trade at such different valuations. The spinner earns what the cotton cycle allows. The brand earns what its name allows.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure on the business, so a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes: fibre and yarn makers, and brands and technical textiles. This is one of the most lopsided radars on any industry page. The yarn shape reaches the full three on rivalry and buyers, two on suppliers and new entrants. The brand shape is a small, even pentagon, scoring one on every spoke.

Look for where the shapes meet. They touch on just one spoke: substitutes, where both score one, because clothes have no substitute and cotton and polyester swap for each other for both groups. Everywhere else, the yarn shape is far bigger.

The biggest gaps are on rivalry and buyers, both three against one. Those two spokes together are the commodity problem: many sellers, price-shopping buyers.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with its reason. Use it to place companies that fall between the two shapes. An export maker sits somewhere in the middle: its buyer spoke is long, because a few large US retailers hold the power, but its rivalry spoke is shorter than a spinner's because qualifying as a big retailer's supplier takes time. An integrated mill shortens the supplier spoke by making its own yarn.

The so-what line puts it in a sentence: profit sits with the brands and specialists, while commodity spinners keep only what the cotton cycle allows.

c10.story:
A textile company's results call can wander through cotton crop estimates, US retailer commentary, freight rates and new spindle counts. Eight numbers cut through it.

Gross margin comes first, because it is the spread between fibre cost and selling price, the core of the business. The benchmarks are very different for spinners and brands, which tells you how different the two businesses are. Operating margin tells you what is left after power, wages and freight.

Then the two working capital numbers that are especially telling in textiles. Inventory days tell you how much cotton and finished stock the company is carrying. A spinner with rising inventory days going into a falling cotton market is sitting on future losses. Receivable days tell you how fast customers pay, and a slowing payer is often an early sign of trouble at a retailer.

The cost lines come next. Power and fuel as a share of sales measures a mill's energy efficiency and the power tariff in its state. Employee cost measures labour intensity: low for an automated spinner, much higher for a garment maker who stitches by hand.

Debt to operating profit is the survival number. Mills that borrowed heavily to carry cotton or build capacity are the ones that struggle in a bust; mills with low debt can buy cheap cotton when others are forced to sell.

Finally, sales growth, but with a twist. In textiles, revenue can rise simply because cotton got more expensive, with no extra volume at all. So the real question is whether sales growth is running ahead of the cotton price change, with volumes up.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: what it tells you, what good looks like and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you: these rows group into spread (gross and operating margin), working capital (inventory and receivable days), cost structure (power and employees), survival (debt) and growth (sales).
  • What good looks like: the benchmark, and the only column with figures. Several rows give different marks for different doors: gross margin separates spinners from brands, operating margin lists spinners, exporters and brands, inventory days separates mills from brands, and employee cost separates spinners from garment makers. Always judge a company against its own door's mark.
  • Today's industry median: from the latest filings of listed textile companies in our database. Every row here has a median, because all eight numbers come straight from standard accounts.

A caution: the median blends spinners, exporters, integrated mills and brands, so it sits somewhere between their benchmarks. It is most useful as a cycle indicator. If the median operating margin is recovering, the industry is recovering.

The best way to use the table is a three-way comparison: the company's own number, the median and its door's good mark. The sales growth row deserves special attention. Compare a company's sales growth with the change in cotton prices over the same period. Growth that merely matches cotton inflation is price, not progress.

c11.story:
The earliest warnings for Indian textiles come from far away: American retailers' inventory reports, US customs data, the global cotton market, the monsoon map, oil prices and Chinese import statistics.

The furthest-reaching signals speak two quarters ahead. US retailers' inventory levels are the most important: lean shelves today mean fresh orders for Indian exporters in six months; bloated shelves mean another lean stretch. Monsoon and cotton sowing data tell you the size of the next crop, and so where cotton prices are heading.

One quarter ahead sits a cluster: US imports of textiles from India show order flow before company results; the global cotton price sets raw material costs and inventory gains or losses; crude oil moves polyester cost and the cotton-polyester balance; and China's yarn imports matter because China is a big buyer of Indian cotton yarn. The rupee works immediately.

Now the rule. This rule is stricter than most: it does not grade on a curve. An up-cycle needs three things together: open market access, Western retailers restocking, and Indian cotton no dearer than the world's. Today only one is in place. Market access has improved dramatically: the US tariff cut, the UK pact live, the EU deal concluded. But US orders are still soft, and Indian cotton is priced high.

So how does that square with a clock reading early up-cycle? The worst is behind the industry, and spinners' margins have recovered, but the full up-cycle the rule describes is not here yet. The access door has opened; customers have not yet walked through it.

Lower tariffs open the door. Only an American restock fills the order book.

That is why the call is cautiously positive, preferring integrated mills and exporters with UK and European reach over pure US home-textile names until US orders clearly recover.
c11.read:
The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot for its channel.

  • Same quarter, far left: the rupee against the dollar, which changes exporters' rupee earnings immediately.
  • One quarter ahead: US imports of textiles from India, the global cotton price, crude oil and China's yarn imports. A busy middle that tells you about next quarter's margins and volumes.
  • Two quarters ahead, furthest right: US retailers' inventory levels and monsoon and cotton sowing. These are the earliest warnings, and the first is the one that will tell you when the exporters' recovery is coming.

Use the chart as a reading order. Start with US retailer inventories: if they are lean and falling, orders are coming. Then check the middle cluster for confirmation: rising US imports from India would be the first hard evidence.

Below the chart sits the rule with its three signs. A tick means the sign is on, a cross means off, and the note gives today's state. Market access: a tick, with the US tariff cut and the UK pact live. Western restocking: a cross, US orders still soft. Competitive cotton: a cross, Indian cotton priced high.
